ca_north_face_14.blurb: The shaded northern side of Fairview Dome, up in Tuolumne Meadows in Yosemite National Park. This is a place for long traditional days: the routes here run from roughly five to twelve pitches, with a spread of grades from 5.9 up through the 5.11s and a single 5.12-level line. Expect a mix of steep cracks, corners and flakes joined by face sections, and a face that stays out of the sun for most of the day. Ten trad lines make it a small but serious venue, best suited to parties comfortable on sustained multi-pitch terrain at altitude.

ca_ant_boulder.blurb: A single boulder, about 17 feet tall, sitting right beside the main path through the Brickyard, the shady sandstone bouldering zone above Santa Barbara. Ten problems share the block, and most of them are friendly: one easy warm-up, a handful at V0 and V1, then a jump to a V4 and a V5 traverse. That makes it a good first stop for newer boulderers and a handy warm-up before moving on to the harder blocks nearby. Bring a pad; the area is compact and busy with other boulders within easy reach.

ct_emc_wall.blurb: A slab roughly 150 feet wide and 90 feet tall at St. John's Ledges near Kent, Connecticut, set apart from the busier main ledges. Ten routes, nearly all traditional with one top-rope line, run from 5.5 up to 5.9. The wall sees few visitors, so the rock tends to be grubby and partly overgrown, and there is no marked trail in; reaching it means a short bushwhack. It suits climbers who like quiet, moderate slab climbing and don't mind a little cleaning, and it rewards people comfortable placing their own gear.

ct_peace_sanctuary.blurb: A small cluster of boulders along a ledge system near Mystic, on Connecticut's coast. The gneiss here is solid and well featured, with edges, pockets and crimps. Ten problems are on offer, from V0 up to a V10, with most of the middle of the range clustered around V3 and V4 and a V7 for those looking up. It is a quiet spot for a short session rather than a big day out, and the coastal climate often keeps the area free of snow in winter and breezy in summer. New lines may still be waiting.

ct_right_wing_wall.blurb: The widest, most open face at Pinnacle Rock in Connecticut's Central Valley, standing to the left of the Cracked Wall and Entertainer Wall. Ten routes, mostly trad with one top-rope, cover 5.5 to 5.9, so it works well for newer leaders and for anyone after steady moderate face climbing on basalt. Protection is sparse on many lines, so confidence on the sharp end helps. Afternoon sun dries the wall quickly after rain but can make summer days hot. Trees up top serve for top-rope anchors, though you will need a long static line to reach them.
